Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Training Large Language Models (LLMs) to understand long contexts requires massive amounts of long-sequence data. However, naturally occurring long documents (such as books or lengthy reports) are statistically scarce in web-scale corpora, which consist primarily of short texts. The current standard solution—mechanically concatenating unrelated short documents to fill a context window—creates "pseudo" long documents. We argue that this approach is fundamentally flawed because tokens separated by vast distances in these concatenated sequences are semantically unrelated. Consequently, models trained on such data struggle to learn genuine long-range dependencies, as there is no incentive for the attention mechanism to attend to distant tokens that are irrelevant to the current generation.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the defining attribute of high-quality long-context data is the density of **long-distance referrals**—instances where a concept mentioned early in the sequence is referenced again significantly later. We posit that simply concatenating random documents dilutes this density.

Our core proposal is that we can synthetically construct high-quality long documents by leveraging the native structure of the web: **hyperlinks**. We believe hyperlinks serve as natural, strong indicators of semantic referrals. By packing web pages together based on their hyperlink connectivity rather than random selection, we can engineer sequences rich in long-distance dependencies, thereby forcing the model to utilize its full context window effectively.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to build a data construction pipeline, tentatively named "LongPack," which assembles long documents by tracing semantic threads through the web graph. The approach focuses on the logical flow of information rather than random sampling.

1.  **Referral-Based Graph Traversal:**
    We will treat the training corpus not as a bag of documents, but as a connected graph. We will select "root" documents (standard web pages) and parse their raw HTML structures to identify outgoing hyperlinks.

2.  **Semantic Pair Extraction:**
    For every hyperlink found in a root document, we identify the **Anchor Text** (the clickable text description) and the **Target Content** (the text of the linked page). The Anchor Text serves as the "key" or "referral" that bridges the two documents.

3.  **Structured Packing Strategy:**
    Instead of appending random text, we will construct a coherent long sequence by aggregating the Target Content associated with a Root Document.
    *   We will retrieve and clean the text of the linked pages.
    *   We will pack these retrieved pages *upstream* (or alongside) the root document within the context window.
    *   Crucially, we will retain the Anchor Text to ensure the model sees the explicit linguistic link between the referenced content (the linked page) and the referring context (the root page).

4.  **Density Optimization:**
    We will prioritize packing chains of documents that maximize the distance between the definition of a concept (in the linked page) and its reference (in the root page), thereby artificially increasing the "long-distance referral density" beyond what is found in standard web text.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Framework:** We aim to establish "referral density" as a critical metric for evaluating long-context data quality, moving beyond simple token counts.
*   **Scalable Data Generation:** This approach provides a method to generate a virtually infinite supply of "near-natural" long documents from existing short-context web corpora, solving the data scarcity bottleneck.
*   **Enhanced Training Efficiency:** By ensuring distant tokens are semantically linked, we expect to train models that actually utilize their extended attention spans for reasoning and retrieval, rather than just tolerating longer input buffers.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a series of experiments to evaluate the impact of long-distance referrals on long-context training and to benchmark the proposed data construction pipeline (LongPack) against existing methods.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Base Pretraining Corpus:** RefinedWeb (public version, 968 million documents, 600 billion tokens).
    *   **Root Documents for Construction:** A subset of RefinedWeb (approx. 5 million documents, 0.5% of the dataset).
    *   **Linked Content Source:** Common Crawl (retrieved HTML based on hyperlinks in root documents).
    *   **Comparison/Baseline Datasets:**
        *   **Books:** Constructed from PG-19.
        *   **Dialogues:** Constructed from public ChatGPT chat history.
        *   **Upsample:** A mixed source dataset created by upsampling long sequence data (threshold 8K tokens) from the pretraining dataset.
        *   **SlimPajama:** Used for calculating validation loss across domains (sampled 10 million tokens per domain).

*   **Model Configuration:**
    *   **Base Model:** GLM-4-9B (9 Billion parameters, rotary position embedding).
    *   **Original Context Length:** 8,192 tokens.
    *   **Target Context Length:** 128,000 tokens.
    *   **Positional Embedding Strategy:** Interpolation with a rotary frequency base increase of 16x (ratio of 128K to 8K).

*   **Training Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** Single node with 8x H100 80GB GPUs.
    *   **Parallelism:** RingAttention for self-attention; DeepSpeed-ZeRO for other components.
    *   **Total Training Tokens:** 1 billion tokens (continuous pre-training/post-training).
    *   **Loss Function:** Standard language modeling loss.
    *   **Hyperparameters:** See Table 3 below.

*   **Evaluation Metrics (RULER Benchmark):**
    *   **Context Length evaluated:** 128K tokens.
    *   **Categories:**
        1.  **Retrieval:** Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) variants. Sub-divided into **Single-pos retrieval** (basic NIAH) and **Multi-pos retrieval** (multiple needles/keys).
        2.  **Multi-hop Tracing:** Variable tracking across the context.
        3.  **Aggregation:** Token-level aggregation (Common Words Extraction, Frequent Words Extraction).
        4.  **Question Answering (QA):** Based on SQuAD and HotpotQA inserted into noise documents.
    *   **Scoring:** Pass rate over 500 samples per task. Reported as category means and an overall weighted average.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Referral Density and Distance Analysis:**
*   We observed that in natural documents, referral density is consistent for distances significantly shorter than the document length but drops sharply when the referral distance approaches the document's total length.
*   We found that simply concatenating short documents does not increase the density of long-distance referrals.
*   Data chunks originating from naturally long documents exhibited a much higher frequency of long-distance referrals compared to concatenated short documents.
*   The "Packed Documents" (constructed via our method) displayed a higher density of very long-distance referrals compared to natural documents, although they showed slightly lower density for short referrals.

**Impact of Document Length on Performance:**
*   Models trained on document groups longer than 8K tokens achieved high scores on basic Needle-In-A-Haystack (NIAH) tests.
*   For complex long-context understanding tasks, performance varied significantly by document length group. Groups trained on longer documents (and thus longer referrals) consistently performed better on "single-pos retrieval," "multi-pos retrieval," and "QA."
*   Performance on "multi-hop tracing" was highest for document groups of 4K-8K and 16K-32K lengths, likely because the task requires summarizing multiple positions which mitigates "lost in the middle" phenomena.
*   We observed that the lower bound of document length acts as a performance bottleneck; using a range of 16K-64K resulted in performance closer to the 16K-32K group rather than the 32K-64K group.

**Impact of Breaking/Enforcing Referrals (Ablation):**
*   **Segmented (Removing long referrals):** When we split 16K-64K documents into 4K segments and distributed them into different chunks (breaking referrals longer than 4K), the overall RULER score dropped by 37.6% (from 53.1 to 33.2). This performance level matched that of the 4K-8K group.
*   **Intra-chunk Reorder (Enhancing long referrals):** When we kept 4K segments in the same chunk but reordered them in a round-robin pattern (forcing referrals to cross segments and become longer), performance improved drastically (33.9% improvement). This provided strong evidence for the importance of long referrals.

**Scalability and Data Construction:**
*   The distribution of document lengths in the RefinedWeb dataset is exponential, with documents exceeding 64K tokens representing less than 0.1% of the dataset.
*   Using our packing pipeline on just 0.5% of RefinedWeb root documents, we generated a dataset equivalent in size to the entire pretraining dataset.
*   The average length of documents increased by 32.7 times through the packing process.
*   Approximately 11.3% of the sampled root pages grew 13 times larger in terms of token count.
*   We successfully scaled the number of root documents and the length of packed documents, indicating high scalability.

**Comparison with Baselines:**
*   Our method outperformed the "Upsample" baseline (previous state-of-the-art recipe) by a significant margin (73.0 vs 55.1 overall score).
*   Our method outperformed domain-specific baselines "Books" and "Dialogues" on most subtasks, particularly retrieval and QA.
*   "Dialogues" performed slightly better than our method on "multi-hop tracing" and "aggregation" (2.4% difference), likely because dialogues inherently consist of assembled independent turns, similar to multi-position tasks.
*   Post-training validation loss across diverse domains (Common Crawl, C4, Github, Wikipedia, etc.) either decreased or remained stable (marginal increase < 1% in C4/Stack-Exchange), indicating that our long-context training did not degrade general model capabilities.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex

\begin{center}
%\framebox[4.0in]{$\;$}
\fbox{\rule[-.5cm]{0cm}{4cm} \rule[-.5cm]{4cm}{0cm}}
\end{center}
\caption{Sample figure caption.}
\end{figure}
```

### Example Code for Tables

```latex
\label{sample-table}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

The capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly defined by their ability to process long contexts (e.g., 32K to 1M tokens) for tasks such as repository-level code completion and retrieval-augmented generation. While attention mechanisms theoretically support these lengths, the quadratic computational complexity makes pretraining on such lengths prohibitively expensive. Consequently, long-context capabilities are typically acquired during a second stage of continuous training.

However, a critical bottleneck exists: **data scarcity**. Natural documents exceeding 64K tokens represent less than 0.1% of standard pretraining datasets. The current standard practice—concatenating short, unrelated documents to fill the context window—creates "pseudo" long documents. We argue that this approach is mechanically sufficient but semantically flawed. Because tokens separated by large distances in concatenated data usually belong to different source documents, they lack semantic dependency. Models trained on such data fail to learn the long-range dependencies required for true long-context understanding. We face a fundamental lack of high-quality, semantically coherent long-sequence data.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that the defining characteristic of high-quality long-context data is the presence of **long-distance referrals**—pairs of tokens that represent the same semantic concept but are separated by significant distance within the sequence.

We posit that the density of these referrals is the primary signal that enables models to learn long-range attention. Therefore, simply upsampling the few existing long documents is insufficient due to their rarity. Instead, we propose **LongPack**, a scalable data construction pipeline. By exploiting the inherent structure of the web—specifically **hyperlinks**—we can artificially construct long documents that maintain or exceed the referral density of natural long documents. By packing web pages together based on their hyperlink connectivity, we can generate a virtually infinite supply of training data that possesses the semantic coherence necessary for effective long-context training.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of Referral Density

To rigorously guide our data construction, we will first quantify the quality of long-context data using the metric of **Referral Density**.

We define an n-gram as $p$, with its semantic meaning denoted as $s(p)$ and its sentence index as $loc(p)$. A **referral** $r$ is defined as a pair of n-grams $(p_1, p_2)$ such that they share the same semantic meaning:
$$ s(p_1) = s(p_2) $$
The **distance** of a referral $d(r)$ is the number of sentences separating the two mentions:
$$ d(r) = loc(p_2) - loc(p_1) $$

We categorize referrals into distance buckets (e.g., 512-2048 sentences). Given a distance threshold $d_0$, we define the **Referral Density** $\Phi'(d_0, doc)$ for a document $doc$ as the count of referrals exceeding that distance, normalized by the document's token length:

$$ \Phi'(d_0, doc) := \frac{| \{ r \mid d(r) \geq d_0, r \in doc \} |}{\mathrm{length}(doc)} $$

Our objective is to construct datasets where $\Phi'(d_0, doc)$ is maximized for large $d_0$, mimicking or surpassing naturally occurring long texts (e.g., books).

### 2. The LongPack Data Pipeline

We will implement **LongPack**, a pipeline to construct coherent long documents from web corpora (e.g., RefinedWeb, RedPajama). We observe that hyperlinks imply a causal or referential relationship, where the anchor text in the source page (the "key") refers to the content of the linked page.

The pipeline will execute the following algorithm:

1.  **Root Page Selection:** We will sample "root pages" from standard pretraining datasets.
2.  **Hyperlink Extraction:** For each root page $r$, we parse the raw HTML to extract hyperlinks. We specifically target the `href` attribute and the anchor text.
    *   Let the anchor text be defined as the **key**.
    *   Let the linked target be the **URL**.
    *   We extract a list of tuples: $[(key_1, URL_1), (key_2, URL_2), \dots]$.
3.  **Content Retrieval:** We query Common Crawl to retrieve the plain text content associated with each $URL_i$.
4.  **Cleaning and Deduplication:** Retrieved pages will undergo standard cleaning (removing HTML metadata). To prevent data repetition which degrades model quality, if multiple root pages refer to the same URL, we will retain the content only for the first occurrence.
5.  **Packing Strategy:** We construct the final long document by prepending the retrieved content *before* the root document.
    *   **Structure:** For a referral $(key, content)$, we format the text as: `key + ":\n" + content`.
    *   **Ordering:** Retrieved contents are ordered based on the appearance of their corresponding hyperlinks in the root page.

### 3. Algorithm Specification

We define the formal data construction process as follows:

**Algorithm: LongPack Data Construction**
```text
Require: Root document r, Root URL u
Require: HTML database H, Cleaned Page database P

html <- look-up(H, u)
references <- regex_substr_all(html, REGEX_REF)
retrieve_target <- []

for r in references do:
    url <- regex_substr(r, REGEX_URL)
    key <- regex_substr(r, REGEX_KEY)
    retrieve_target.append((url, key))
end for

retrieve_target <- dedup_url_merge_key(retrieve_target)
packed_document <- ""

for (url, keys) in retrieve_target do:
    content <- look_up(P, url)
    # Prepend anchor text as a header
    packed_document <- packed_document + keys + ":\n" + content
end for

final_document <- packed_document + r
```

We will employ strict regex filtering to ensure only meaningful semantic links are captured, discarding navigation bars or footer links which do not represent semantic referrals.

### 4. Training Configuration

We will validate this data by fine-tuning a pretrained transformer (e.g., GLM-4-9B). The training will utilize:
*   **Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) Interpolation:** To adapt the model from a short pretrained context (e.g., 8K) to a target context (e.g., 128K), we will scale the rotary frequency by a factor $k$, where $k = \frac{\text{target\_length}}{\text{original\_length}}$.
*   **Sequence Parallelism:** We will utilize RingAttention to manage the memory costs of long-sequence activations.

## Expected Contribution

This research is expected to provide a definitive solution to the data bottleneck in long-context LLM training.

1.  **Theoretical Contribution:** We will establish **Referral Density** as the critical metric for evaluating long-context data quality, shifting the focus from mere token count to semantic connectivity.
2.  **Methodological Contribution:** LongPack will demonstrate that high-quality long documents can be synthesized from short web pages. By utilizing only a fraction (e.g., 0.5%) of a standard pretraining corpus as root documents, we expect to generate a massive corpus of long-context data (equivalent to the size of the entire pretraining dataset) without relying on rare, naturally long documents.
3.  **Performance Improvement:** We anticipate that models trained on LongPack data will significantly outperform those trained on simple concatenated chunks or standard upsampling methods, particularly on tasks requiring retrieval and multi-hop reasoning over distances exceeding 32K tokens.

notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
